articles.title: After losing their Los Angeles home in the wildfire, a California family bought a $1 historic house and moved it onto their burned property
articles.summary: US News: A California family has found a unique way to rebuild after losing its Altadena home in the devastating Eaton fire. Instead of constructing a new hous.
articles.body: A California family has found a unique way to rebuild after losing its Altadena home in the devastating Eaton fire. Instead of constructing a new house, it bought a nearly 100-years-old historic home for just $1 and moved it to the burned property. The house, nicknamed ‘Pinky,’ was facing demolition in Hollywood before the family stepped in to save it. The 2,500-square-foot Tudor Revival home was divided into two sections, transported 26 miles by truck and placed on the family’s empty lot. This remarkable move is part of the ‘Historic House Relocation Project,’ an initiative designed to preserve older Los Angeles homes while helping families displaced by wildfires. For the Martinez family, this solution offered a larger home filled with historic character, while giving an endangered house another chance to become part of a community again.How did a $1 house become new home for the California familyLauren Martinez and her husband learned about the Historic House Relocation Project, launched by Los Angeles architecture firm ‘Omgivning’ in 2025. The project finds older homes that are facing demolition and matches them with families rebuilding after the wildfires. The idea is relatively simple, even if the actual work is not. A house that might otherwise be demolished is purchased, carefully taken apart or divided into sections, transported to another property and then restored. For the Martinezes, the right house was a nearly 100-years-old Tudor Revival property in Hollywood. It had been well maintained and still featured hardwood floors throughout. The one-storey house measured about 2,500 square feet and contained four bedrooms and three bathrooms. Most remarkably, the family bought it for only $1. They gave the house a nickname ‘Pinky’ that reflected how quickly it became part of the family and because it was pink inside and out. Martinez said that the house felt as though it carried years of love and character with it.What happened to the Martinez family’s original homeThe Martinez family had lived in their Altadena home for 8 years and were raising their children, when the Eaton fire destroyed it in January 2025. Lauren Martinez was eight months pregnant with her third child when she received messages warning her to stay away from the neighbourhood. The following day, her husband saw the smouldering rubble of their family home. The family later found themselves living in a rental while considering how to rebuild. But the financial reality made a traditional replacement difficult. According to Realtor, Martinez said insurance would not have provided enough money to recreate the home they had lost at the same size. Building again would have meant accepting a smaller, simpler house. That pushed the family to consider a very different option of moving an existing historic house onto their land.Moving an entire house across Los AngelesMoving a house is considerably more complicated than transporting ordinary furniture. The Martinez project required months of planning involving architects, contractors and specialist movers. The house had to be divided along what was considered its most suitable natural seam. Omgivning creative director ‘Morgan Sykes Jaybush’ compared the process to slicing a loaf of bread. Each half then had to be prepared for transport and moved separately. On 12 January 2026, the first half was secured with wood, mounted on steel beams and placed on a flatbed tractor-trailer. It travelled 26 miles from Hollywood to Altadena during the night. Four days later, the second half made the same journey. The Los Angeles Conservancy reports that the wider Historic House Relocation Project requires careful evaluation and documentation before a house is moved. Once relocated, each property needs a new foundation and must be rehabilitated to meet modern building codes while retaining its historic character.Relocation, instead of demolition of the historic houses The project is tackling two problems at once. According to the Los Angeles Conservancy, many older homes in LA face demolition as neighbourhoods change and redevelopment takes place. At the same time, families affected by the Eaton and Palisades fires need ways to rebuild without losing the character of their communities. The relocation project connects those two needs. Rather than allowing an older house to disappear, it gives the building a new site and a new family. The Los Angeles Conservancy reports that three early relocations include the 1911 Chambers Residence, the 1910 Duntley-Blackburn Residence and the 1926 Martinez Residence. According to Realtor, Omgivning has helped three families relocate homes so far, while around 200 people are on its waiting list. The project’s organisers estimate that the approach can be about 20% cheaper than constructing a new home on average, while also saving older houses from demolition.What happens to ‘Pinky’ nextAlthough the house has reached the Martinez family’s Altadena property, the work is far from finished. The building is currently resting on temporary supports while a new foundation is prepared. Plumbing and electrical systems must be installed, the two sections need to be joined, and the roof, which was removed before the move, must be rebuilt. The kitchen will also be renovated. Martinez expects the entire project to cost between $900,000-$950,000. Even so, she believes building a new house from scratch would have taken longer and potentially cost considerably more. Most importantly, the relocated home gives the family the character of an older house. After watching their old home disappear in the fire, they are now waiting for a house with its own history to become their new beginning.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Haweswater barn loft transformed to support bat colony
articles.summary: A Lake District barn is restored to house both its brown long-eared bat colony and RSPB visitors.
articles.body:
A barn loft has been transformed to support its resident colony of brown long-eared bats.

The RSPB secured a £135,000 grant to restore a traditional Cumbrian spinning barn - a site where farm workers spun sheep's wool - into a visitor's hub and conserve its bat colony in its loft at Wild Haweswater near Penrith.

The site's manager, Annabel Rushton, said the bats were named because they had "fantastic lugs on them", and were among soprano pipistrelle, common pipistrelle and Daubenton's bats at the site.

Rushton said there had been more entrances and exits created, more "nooks and crannies for them to hide in and roost" and the building was heated ahead of hibernation.

"The barn was previously a dark, dilapidated place with rotten beams, meaning the bats did not have place to rest and roost," Rushton said.

"All bats are up against a lot of challenges that many of our wildlife in the UK are also facing, for example a decline in insects."

Rushton said the mammals were "very special" and it was "great to be able to support them" at the barn, which is owned by United Utilities.

The grant from FCC Communities Foundation has also enabled a full restoration of the indoor space below the loft.

The hub will host groups and public events, where people can learn more about the landscape recovery work being undertaken in the Haweswater area.

articles.title: Meet Kim Ji-on, a 12-year-old South Korean student who invented a life-saving device that helps people escape deadly fires
articles.summary: Rest of World News: What's the one thing you would carry to a remote island with you? If honesty is the way forward, most would say their phone. While there was a time so.
articles.body: What's the one thing you would carry to a remote island with you? If honesty is the way forward, most would say their phone. While there was a time someone would have said an answer like a weapon or maybe their loved one, now, it is truly a mobile phone that lives rent-free with a person everywhere they go, especially during emergencies. And what if it was these phones that could not only help you communicate during such times but also save your lives? This is a question a 12-year-old South Korean teenager asked herself.When it comes to fires, an estimated 8 million incidents happen annually. While on paper, everyone knows to stay low and cover their face with a wet towel to protect themselves from smoke and toxic gases, not all lives are saved by the strategy, as people are left unconscious before the flames get to them. What if you could use something that you carry everywhere with you?According to The Korea Herald, Kim Ji-on saw a news story two years ago about a fire at a hotel in Bucheon that killed seven people. The victims, trapped on site, made final calls to their families, which got her thinking about what could have helped them survive the tragedy.The answer arrived when she visited a local fire station during a school field trip and had a eureka moment. Upon learning from a firefighter that smoke and toxic fumes incapacitate people, she came up with the idea of putting a protective filter into the grip on cell phone cases.Fire safety guidelines often advise people to cover their nose and mouth with a wet towel, but Kim thought that someone waking up to a fire might have little time to find a towel and soak it in water. “I thought that if we kept protective gear attached to a smartphone, something people carry with them all the time and even keep by their side while they sleep, more people could make it out safely in an emergency,” she explained to a local news outlet.With the help of her teachers at the Chilcheon Elementary School in Geoje, South Gyeongsang Province, Kim Ji-on turned her idea into a successful reality. She fitted a collapsible phone grip with activated carbon fibre and a nonwoven filter. These materials, respectively, absorb harmful gases and trap fine particles. In the event of a fire, the device, when unfolded, can be placed over the nose and mouth and the user can safely breathe, at least for a while she acknowledges.“It may not protect you for as long as a real gas mask, but I think it can give you those crucial first one or two minutes to get out,” Kim said.The fire-escape breathing phone grip won the Presidential Award, the top honour at the nation's 2026 Youth Invention Festival, beating out entries by older middle and high school students. Kim plans to donate her 3 million won ($2,120) prize money to help people in developing countries. Launched in 1988, the annual festival has grown into the country’s largest invention event for young people. This year’s competition attracted 6,959 entries, of which 183 were selected for honours.The school Kim goes to is a small one on Chilchendo Island in Geoje, with just 20 students across six classes and ten teachers. Despite its size, the school produced four winners at the competition, including Kim, with three other students taking gold, silver and bronze prizes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: New Wolverhampton home means 'big ambitions' for wood enterprise
articles.summary: Wolverhampton Wood Recycling's bigger premises will bring more volunteers together, its founders say.
articles.body:
A wood recycling group's move to bigger premises means "bigger ambitions" and helping more people volunteer and learn new skills, its founders said.

Wolverhampton Wood Recycling (WWR) turns waste wood into a range of items for sale and offers a bespoke service, thanks to its team of volunteers from its new home on Webner Industrial Estate in Wolverhampton.

The larger space will lead to more community activities and new projects designed to bring people together, including plans for a Repair café and a Men's Shed, Jim Brennan from the social enterprise said.

"We want this to be a place where people can come along, learn, share their skills, meet others and feel that they belong," he said.

Brennan launched the community interest company with co-founder Eimert De Graff with about nine volunteers at the end of last year.

"When we started, we knew we wanted to do something about wood waste, but we also knew there was an opportunity to do something much bigger for our community," Brennan added.

"The move to bigger [premises] means we can take on more wood, but it also means we can welcome more people."

The organisation liaises with businesses and construction companies to collect, sort and recycle their wood waste, "giving materials a new lease of life wherever possible".

Visitors will be able to buy a wider selection of reclaimed wood, as well as items such as benches, bin stores and planters.

The group is particularly keen to support people who may be experiencing loneliness, retirement or living with health condition which affected their day-to-day life.

Gordon, who has volunteered with WWR since its inception, said: "I am a skilled wood machinist living with health conditions that currently limit my ability to undertake paid employment.

"I started volunteering because I wanted something to do and to get out of the house. I never expected it to become such an important part of my week.

"You meet people, you have a laugh, you learn things and feel like you're contributing."

De Graff said he was also excited at plans for the Repair Cafe and Men's Shed as they would bring people together.

"There are so many people in our communities who have incredible practical skills and experience but don't always have somewhere to use them," he said.

articles.title: Fears over Burscough 'high risk' crossing after train crash death
articles.summary: An investigation is ongoing into the cause of a crash in which a delivery driver was killed on a crossing.
articles.body:
An investigation is continuing into how a delivery vehicle and a train collided on a crossing, killing a van driver.

The incident happened off Martin Lane and Whitehouse Lane in Burscough, West Lancashire, on Saturday at about 15:00 GMT, when a train from Southport to Manchester collided with what is understood to be a supermarket delivery vehicle.

People living in the area have told the BBC that it was not uncommon for the gate on the crossing to be left open at times by people using it.

The claims have been put to Network Rail, which, while not able to comment on the claims, said it was involved in an investigation alongside British Transport Police and the Rail Accident Investigation Board.

The train was travelling towards Burscough town centre when the collision happened. A woman who was on board the train described seeing the van travelling along Martin Lane before it collided with the Northern train.

The crossing where the crash took place is not a full level crossing, but one operated by people as and when they use it.

It has lights and makes warning noises when the gate is not shut.

One man familiar with the area told the BBC that the gate was regularly left open.

He said from his experience the crossing was mainly used by locals and farmers, but that he was seeing more delivery drivers using it lately.

He added: "We really hope that there will be some sort of automated gate there that can only be opened by the public… the gate is always left open and we know that because we are often down there. I have flagged it to Network Rail."

The man said there had been a CCTV camera on the crossing for a number of years.

The crossing is classed as a "user-worked crossing with miniature stop lights" and has a risk rating of B4, which Network Rail categorises as having a "high individual risk" and a "very high collective risk".

A woman at a nearby business said "people who use it are aware… to open and close it", but said there were "so few people who used it".

But the man told us that there had been a notable increase in the number of delivery drivers in the area in recent years, and that the hedge running along Martin Lane was high and might not offer a clear view of trains coming down the track at all times.

Sophie Cassidy, 26, who was on the train with her two small children when the collision happened, said she had seen the vehicle approaching.

She and other passengers on the train were lifted down to safety by police, fire and paramedic crews about two hours after the crash.

She said: "I can't put into words how lucky we are to be alive. I'm still trying to wrap my mind around it all."

More than 24 hours after the collision, the line remains closed and the train remains on the tracks while investigations are carried out.

A Network Rail spokesman said: "Following an incident at a level crossing in Burscough, the line between Wigan and Southport remains closed.

"Alongside Northern, we are supporting both the British Transport Police and the Rail Accident Investigation Branch with their investigations."

A British Transport Police (BTP) spokesman said: "Enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances of what happened."

articles.title: Did US military warn Hegseth over Iran war strain before latest escalation? What report claims
articles.summary: US News: Several senior US military leaders reportedly warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that prolonging large-scale operations against Iran was unsustaina.
articles.body: Several senior US military leaders reportedly warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that prolonging large-scale operations against Iran was unsustainable and could weaken the military’s ability to respond to threats elsewhere, including against the US homeland.The assessment was prepared for Hegseth and recorded in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB), weeks before the latest escalation in fighting between the United States and Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal citing sources. It reflected concerns over the continued deployment of US forces to the Middle East as the Iran conflict entered its sixth month.The heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force, along with the four-star commanders overseeing US operations in Europe, Asia and Latin America, raised concerns over the strain the prolonged operation was placing on troops, equipment and military readiness, the people said.The SDOB, typically produced twice a month, tracks the worldwide availability of US warships, aircraft, personnel and weapons systems and helps inform Pentagon decisions on force deployments.At the time of the assessment, US Central Command had more than 50,000 troops on alert in the region as President Donald Trump continued to demand that Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept US terms for ending the conflict. Trump had also kept open the possibility of further military action.The August 14 orders book directed some forces in the Middle East to remain deployed through September and others into 2027. That prospect prompted several senior commanders to formally object to extending their forces, while saying they would carry out the orders.The commanders of US European Command, US Pacific Command and US Southern Command, along with the Navy's top admiral, issued what the document described as a “non-concur”; indicating disagreement with the deployment extensions but an intention to execute them.The military leaders warned that the Iran operation was drawing ships, aircraft and other equipment away from other theatres, limiting their ability to conduct missions and maintain training.Army and Air Force leadership agreed with extending their deployments but warned that doing so carried significant risks.Overall, the assessment described the Iran operation as “too much for too long,” according to one person familiar with it, as quoted by WSJ.Navy under mounting strainThe Navy has borne a particularly heavy burden, supplying dozens of vessels for the Iran campaign, including for combat operations, defence against Iranian attacks and the enforcement of Trump's blockade of Iranian ports.Some ship and crew deployments had already been extended by months.Adm. Daryl Caudle, the chief of Naval Operations, told Hegseth that the Navy could not sustain its current level of support for the Iran conflict because there was no anticipated end date, according to people familiar with the assessment.Caudle also indicated that barely one-fourth of the Navy's destroyer fleet was ready to deploy, a sharp decline from prewar levels. Continued demands from the Iran operation were also jeopardising ship maintenance and the fleet's availability for other potential conflicts.At a recent event in Norfolk, Caudle described the deployment extensions as “very challenging for our sailors.”“I typically am not a big fan of extensions, and I push back hard on that, but the enemy gets a vote,” he said, according to a Navy transcript.The strain was also being felt by other branches of the military.The commanders of European and Southern commands warned that providing ships and surveillance aircraft to Central Command had degraded their ability to fulfil homeland-defence responsibilities.Adm Samuel Paparo, head of Pacific Command, objected to the level of support his command was continually required to provide, including an aircraft carrier strike group and destroyers.The Army was also preparing to extend deployments. Elements of the 82nd Airborne Division, which mobilised 2,000 soldiers in March in response to the Iran war, were set for deployments lasting up to a year. Those troops would be central to any potential ground invasion of Iran.Units operating Patriot air-defence systems were also expected to have their deployments extended.The prolonged war has meanwhile depleted key U.S. military stocks. The Pentagon has faced shortages of Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors, as well as long-range Tomahawk missiles. About 25% of the Pentagon's Reaper drone fleet had also been lost, while U.S. bases in the Middle East had suffered billions of dollars in damage, according to earlier reports.The Trump administration has rejected reports that the U.S. is facing significant munitions shortages.Latest escalation came despite warnings?The concerns in the August 14 assessment predated the latest escalation in the US-Iran conflict, which means the most recent US strikes on Larak Island late Sunday and promopting Iran's retaliation.The assessment nevertheless highlights the military readiness dilemma facing the Trump administration: sustaining a prolonged campaign against Iran could leave fewer forces and weapons available to respond to other threats, particularly in Europe and the Indo-Pacific.A Pentagon spokesman said decisions on the scope and duration of deployments are based on the current threat assessment, presidential priorities and advice from senior military commanders.The Pentagon declined to discuss the SDOB or specific “concurrences, non-concurrences, or risk assessments” provided during force-allocation deliberations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1600s, people in Osaka ate dozens of species of fish, mammals and plants; 400 years later scientists found the evidence trapped in their teeth
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Four centuries ago, the people living in Osaka left behind an unlikely record of what they ate. It was not written in a cookbook or preserved in a mar.
articles.body: Four centuries ago, the people living in Osaka left behind an unlikely record of what they ate. It was not written in a cookbook or preserved in a market ledger, but in the hardened deposits that accumulated on their teeth. Scientists have now analysed ancient dental calculus from eight people buried at the Ofuka-cho site, also known as the Umeda cemetery, in Osaka. By extracting and identifying ancient proteins trapped inside the calculus, researchers reconstructed parts of the diets of ordinary people living in premodern Osaka. The study identified 38 dietary proteins belonging to 17 taxa, revealing a surprisingly varied menu that included fish, terrestrial mammals and plant products. Among the findings were economically valuable red sea bream, salmonids that had travelled long distances, mammalian meat and proteins from cottonseed, potentially reflecting the use of cottonseed oil. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the food actually reaching ordinary people in Osaka hundreds of years ago.What did people in premodern Osaka eat?The research was published in Anthropological Science under the title ‘Dietary reconstruction of individual premodern commoners in Osaka, Japan, through the palaeoproteomic analysis of human dental calculus.’ The authors are Yoko Uchida-Fukuhara, Mariko Iida, Shigenobu Oba, Rikai Sawafuji, Takumi Nishiuchi, Shiori Fujisawa, Tomohito Nagaoka and Takumi Tsutaya. The paper was published online on August 19, 2026. Rather than examining food remains alone, the researchers focused on dental calculus, the mineralised material that forms when plaque accumulates on teeth. This material can preserve proteins from foods consumed by an individual, allowing scientists to investigate diet at a much more specific level than conventional archaeological methods. The analysis found proteins from 17 different taxa. Fish were particularly prominent, with proteins from nine types of fish identified in the broader research findings. These included red sea bream (Pagrus major), a relatively high-value fish, as well as salmonids. The presence of salmonid proteins is especially significant because these fish were traded over long distances. Their discovery suggests that the people buried at the site could access food transported from distant regions, rather than relying solely on resources available around Osaka.Ancient teeth reveal a surprisingly diverse food supplyOne of the most striking discoveries was evidence for terrestrial mammals. Four of the eight individuals analysed had proteins originating from non-human terrestrial or marine mammals. This is particularly interesting because meat from four-legged terrestrial animals is often associated with dietary restrictions in premodern Japan, influenced partly by Buddhist beliefs and concepts surrounding pollution. However, historical evidence suggests that meat was not completely absent from Japanese diets. Wild animals could be consumed under the practice known as kusurigui, or “medicinal eating”, in which meat was sometimes framed as having therapeutic value. The new dental-calculus evidence provides something different: a direct biological indication that some people living in premodern Osaka had actually consumed terrestrial mammal meat. Historical records also document the sale of venison in Osaka during the later Edo period. The study therefore adds another layer to the picture of food consumption. What might appear from written customs to have been a restricted or unusual food could nevertheless have reached the tables of some urban residents. The researchers also detected proteins associated with cottonseed. Cotton seeds themselves are not normally eaten because they contain compounds that can be toxic, but cottonseed could be processed to produce edible oil. The finding therefore potentially reflects the use of cottonseed oil as part of food preparation.Why Osaka gave ordinary people access to so many foodsThe diversity revealed in the teeth appears to be closely connected to Osaka's role as a major distribution centre. Premodern Osaka was known as the “Kitchen of the Realm”, a reputation linked to its extensive networks for collecting, transporting and distributing food. The city functioned as a logistical hub through which products from different parts of Japan could move into urban markets. The study's central distinction is between food supply and food accessibility. Finding evidence that a particular food existed somewhere in a region does not necessarily mean that everyone could obtain it. The proteins preserved in the teeth provide evidence that at least some commoners actually had access to a surprisingly broad selection of foods. This is important because the individuals studied were not members of an elite household. The researchers describe them as commoners, including people who were relatively economically disadvantaged. Yet their dental calculus shows that their diets could include foods with very different geographical and economic origins. In other words, Osaka's sophisticated transport and market networks appear to have brought dietary diversity well beyond the wealthiest sections of society.How can scientists reconstruct a 400-year-old diet from teeth?Traditional archaeological techniques can reveal much about past diets, but they have limitations. Animal bones can show which species were present at a settlement, while stable isotope analysis can indicate broad patterns such as the importance of marine foods or terrestrial plants. Dental calculus provides a different kind of evidence. As plaque mineralises into calculus, microscopic biological material can become trapped within it. In this study, researchers used palaeoproteomics, analysing ancient proteins preserved in the calculus. By comparing the protein sequences with reference databases, they could identify food sources at a much more detailed taxonomic level. The team also combined the dental-calculus analysis with carbon and nitrogen stable-isotope analysis of bone collagen. The isotope results were consistent with previously reported patterns for premodern Japanese commoners, while the protein evidence added much greater detail about individual food items. That combination allowed the researchers to move from a broad question, whether people relied heavily on marine or terrestrial resources, towards a more specific one: which foods were actually reaching individual people? The teeth essentially became tiny archaeological archives.What the findings reveal about Edo-period food cultureThe discovery does more than reconstruct a menu. It provides evidence about how an urban food system worked and who benefited from it. The presence of valuable fish, distant salmonids, terrestrial animal products and plant-derived ingredients suggests that food networks in Osaka were capable of supplying ordinary residents with resources originating from very different places. The researchers argue that this accessibility helped shape Japan's culinary culture and highlights the important role played by commoners in its development. The study also demonstrates why ancient dental calculus is becoming an increasingly valuable source for archaeologists. A person's teeth can survive long after written memories of their everyday life have disappeared. Hidden inside those teeth may be molecular traces of meals, trade networks and food choices. Four hundred years later, the hardened residue left behind after ordinary meals has provided scientists with an unusually intimate record of life in historic Osaka, one bite at a time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Melinda French Gates donated $10M to Olivia Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields Festival, bringing the total to $20M, here's where the money will be going
articles.summary: US News: Trust the women in the world to make change and they will. Singer, songwriter Olivia Rodrigo successfully concluded her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields F.
articles.body: Trust the women in the world to make change and they will. Singer, songwriter Olivia Rodrigo successfully concluded her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Festival on Saturday, August 29, in Irvine, California. The star-studded event included performances from artists such as Stevie Nicks, Karen O, Chappell Roan, Doechii, Bikini Kill, Rachel Chinouriri, Garbage, The Breeders and Mitski.The festival was inspired by Lilith Fair, which was co-founded by Sarah McLachlan in 1997 in response to the misogyny she and her peers were facing in the music industry. At the event, Rodrigo announced that they had raised $20M for women-focused organisations, aided by a donation from Melinda French Gates.Before she began her performance, Rodrigo thanked all of the musicians who took part in the festival: “The fact that they took the time out of their insanely busy schedules to come and do this festival for free is something I’m so grateful for,” she said. “Because of that, and because of all of you who came to hang out today, I can stand on the stage and say we are donating $10m to 10 incredible charities. I really believe that giving women the tools to decide their own futures and live healthy lives free of violence and discrimination is the most effective tool we have at changing the world for the better.”Rodrigo then introduced Melinda French Gates, praising her as “one of the most inspiring women I’ve ever met”. “She’s devoted her life to empowering women and girls that might have otherwise been forgotten,” Rodrigo said. “She’s generous and brave and has done so much good in this world, and I’m totally floored because as well as being in attendance here tonight, she’s pledged to double every dollar that we made here today to a grand total of funds being donated to $20m. I’m so grateful!”Funds raised through the festival will be split equally among 10 beneficiary organisations: Baby2Baby, Black Mamas Matter Alliance, Centre for Reproductive Rights, FreeFrom, Jhpiego, John Hopkins Centre for Indigenous Health, National Domestic Workers Alliance, National Institute for Reproductive Health, National Women’s Law Centre, and Planned Parenthood.Here's what the organisations do:Baby2Baby provides children in need with diapers, clothing and basic necessities.Black Mamas Matter Alliance aims to address maternal health inequities among Black women and improve their maternal healthCentre for Reproductive Rights is a legal organisation protecting reproductive rights and reproductive health globallyFreeFrom works to end gender-based violence and offers programs centred around finances and cash assistanceJhpeigo aims to improve access to critical health care globallyJohns Hopkins Centre for Indigenous Health promotes health equity for Indigenous peopleNational Domestic Workers Alliance works to win labour rights and protections for domestic workersNational Institute for Reproductive Health partners with state and local advocates to provide strategic guidance, support and funding for access to reproductive health careNational Women's Law Centre advocates for 'gender justice' through courts and in public policyPlanned Parenthood provides sexual and reproductive health care for people nationwideRodrigo said the organisations are doing "incredibly important work every single day in the U.S. and globally." "I'm so grateful to every person who bought a ticket, every artist who waived their fee, every sponsor for signing onto a brand new festival and every donation that helped get to $10 million to support women and girls," she said.The event came as US President Donald Trump attempted to overhaul family planning grants that reproductive health clinics used to provide birth control and treat sexually transmitted infections. His administration paused $27.5 million last year for such organisations, including some Planned Parenthood affiliates, before officials agreed to restore the money.Rodrigo and her festival co-organisers have hinted that the event will return, as a post to its Instagram page showed the huge crowds in attendance with the caption: “One year down, and we’ll just keep growing.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: After Pakistan, Uzbekistan gets China’s J-10 fighter; Bangladesh could be next
articles.summary: International News: The Uzbek Air Force, has taken procession of its first J-10CE from China. This makes Uzbekistan the second country after Pakistan to operate the multi.
articles.body: The Uzbek Air Force, has taken procession of its first J-10CE from China. This makes Uzbekistan the second country after Pakistan to operate the multi-role fighter aircraft developed by the Chengdu Aircraft Corporation (CAC). The aircraft were seen landing in the country just before the country marks its 35th independence day. Uzbekistan is reported to have ordered as many has 24 J-10s, of which at least six have been delivered to the central Asian nation. At the same time Pakistan is said to operate as many as 20 aircraft and China's People's Liberation Army Air Force operating a little over 600 of these aircraft. Bangladesh, too is likely to procure this aircraft and has started the process to acquire the single engine Chinese aircraft.This comes at a time when China’s defence exports have declined despite a rise in global arms procurement. The rise is driven largely by Europe’s response to the Ukraine war. Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) notes China’s share of the global defence market has dropped, with Pakistan absorbing most of its exports and Bangladesh taking a smaller share.The appeal of the J-10The J-10, known as 'Vigorous Dragon' in China, is ana advanced fighter aircraft comparable to fourth-generation fighter aircraft offered by western nations and Russia. The newer versions of the aircraft ae equipped with some of the latest sensors and avionics. This sophisticated suite consists of an advanced Active Electronically Scanned Array radar and an infrared search and track system, that can track aircraft through the target aircraft's thermal signature.The aircraft is armed with air-to-air weapons such as the beyond visual range PL-15 missile. Some of these missiles, fired by Pakistani aircraft, were recovered intact in the fields of Punjab during the active phase of Operation Sindoor. The Chinese variant of the aircraft are also armed with the extremely long-ranged PL-17 missile, which has an advertised range of over 400 km and is designed to bring down large and less maneuverable force multipliers such as AEW&CS aircraft and aerial refuelling platforms. The aircraft also deploy different types of air to surface weapons such as missiles and bombsChina's J-10C may not be Beijing's most advanced fighter, but it could well be its most consequential in terms of exports. The single-engine jet combines an agile airframe with long-range missile integration and modern avionics in its C-variant, all at a fraction of the cost of heavier twin-engine fighters. Its drawbacks, limited range compared to heavier platforms, single-engine survivability concerns, historical reliance on Russian engines and high radar observability, are real but haven't stopped it from becoming a workhorse. Expected to serve for decades as a high-low complement to the stealthy J-20, the J-10C represents China's gradual break from foreign dependence and its rise as a serious aerospace power.For air forces like Bangladesh's, still flying ageing Chengdu F-7s and a handful of MiG-29s, the J-10CE offers a considerable leap. Maintaining Soviet-era fleets has grown harder by the year, with airframe fatigue, dwindling spare parts and shrinking Russian reliability, worsened by the Ukraine war and sanctions, all weighing on readiness. Chinese jets offer a way around these constraints, arriving bundled with weapons, training and support, without the political strings that often accompany Western defence deals.

articles.title: Early release scheme could still see dangerous criminals released, Conservatives warn
articles.summary: The warning comes after the prime minister said some prisoners serving indefinite sentences could be freed to increase prison capacity.
articles.body:
Dangerous criminals could be freed under the government's early release scheme for England and Wales, the Conservatives have warned.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy told the BBC that to prevent one group of dangerous criminals being released early, Andy Burnham was "looking at releasing a different group of dangerous prisoners".

The prime minister said at the weekend anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the early prisoner release scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

He said prison space would be found by releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences, known as IPPs as well as by deporting foreign prisoners.

Prisoners freed early are returning to jail at rapid rate, governors tell BBC

Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?

On Monday Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones told the BBC: "We will do nothing that would risk the public or put the public at danger."

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being released in tranches from October to ease overcrowding in jails.

The numbers due to be released has been reduced after the government said rapists, those found guilty of serious child sex offences and grooming offences and now those found guilty of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme.

Given that fewer prisoners will now be released than initially expected this will have a knock-on effect on prison capacity.

Timothy said releasing prisoners serving indefinite sentences under imprisonment for public protection sentences posed its own risk.

Between 2005 and 2012 IPPs were given to some offenders in England and Wales where they were considered to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once they had served a minimum term they could only be released once the Parole Board was satisfied they no longer posed a risk to the public. Although IPPs are no longer imposed many people already serving sentences are stlll in prison.

Timothy told the BBC: "By definition, the people who are still in prison on those sentences are dangerous, because they've all been considered by independent expert assessors who have concluded that they are not safe to release and they would be a danger to the public."

He accepted not enough prisons had been built under the previous Conservative government.

Indefinite prison sentences have previously been handed out in several high-profile cases, including to Tracey Connelly, the mother of Baby P, who was jailed in 2009 after admitting causing or allowing the death of her one-year-old son Peter.

There were 2,271 people serving IPPs, according to Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data up to June this year.

Of those, 856 have never been released because the Parole Board thought it was not safe to do so. Ending indefinite sentences for those still serving them would require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.

Davies-Jones told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "The government's number one priority is to keep the public safe and in order to do that we need a functioning criminal justice system."

She defended the government's decision to look at indefinite sentences as part of ensuring there were enough prison spaces.

"We need to look at every case on its merits individually, and pass the appropriate legislation and we will do that responsibly and we will take our time to get it right," she added.

She said those released would still be monitored.

Speaking exclusively to BBC Breakfast on Sunday, Burnham said he had applied "common sense" on IPPs.

"I was faced with a situation where people on those sentences who have more than served their time, not being released when others who've committed very serious crimes being released early," he said.

He said the government would table legislation to terminate IPPs by the end of this Parliament.

He conceded that of those offenders, there would be those who would "pose a risk to communities", and a cross-party oversight group would be established.

And there are others who have a more favourable outlook about releasing some prisoners serving IPPs.

Former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland told the Today programme that while there are people serving these indefinite sentences who are a "real danger to the public", these are "dwarfed" by instances where people end up back in prison for things like breaching their strict licence conditions.

One such person is Shaun Lloyd, who served eight years following a conviction for street robbery.

Once released, because of his IPP, he remained on indefinite licence. People on these could be recalled for behaviour that, while not criminal, would be in breach of those rules.

His mother, Shirley Debon, told the Today programme that he had never committed a violent crime and called his latest recall "totally unfair".

When Lloyd was called back to prison, he had become drug-free and was near to completing an apprenticeship, she said.

Debon is campaigning more broadly for an inquiry into IPPs, under which she says people are "living in limbo".

Sir Robert said that looking at recall cases like Lloyd's could be a solution for the government.

He added that there was "a very good policy reason" why IPPs were abolished: "It did create uncertainty, not just for the prisoners but actually for the victims".

On the impact overall of changes to the early release scheme for prisons, Davies-Jones told the BBC: "We will have capacity within the system with those numbers but it will be run very tight."

She said plans to deport foreign nationals on sentencing and to re-purpose women's prisons would help tackle overcrowding.

"Our plan is to deport [foreign nationals] on sentencing so that they don't serve a day at his Majesty's and at the taxpayers pleasure."

Asked if these offenders would serve sentences for their crimes once deported, she said "that would be for the determination of their country of origin".

On 3 August, the prison population in England and Wales was 86,495, around 97% of useable capacity.

On Tuesday, Justice Secretary Alex Norris is expected update Parliament with further details on the changes to the early release scheme.

articles.title: Nearly one in three voters struck off Delhi SIR draft roll
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Nearly one in three registered voters of Delhi have been struck off the draft Special Intensive Revision (SIR) electoral roll which was pub.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Nearly one in three registered voters of Delhi have been struck off the draft Special Intensive Revision (SIR) electoral roll which was published by Election Commission Monday morning.The draft rolls include the names of 97,53,577 voters while names of 47,56,722 among 1.45 crore registered voters are missing from the SIR rolls because they failed to submit their voter details during the one and a half month long voters verification exercise conducted across 70 assembly constituencies of the capital.Election officials said many voters were not found at their registered addresses, while others had shifted within Delhi or moved out of the city.According to figures released by the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer, enumeration forms of 67.2% of Delhi’s electorate were submitted and digitised. The remaining 32.8% were categorised as Absent, Shifted, Dead, Duplicate and Others (ASDDO).TOI on July 26 reported that around 20% of the registered voters were not found at their addresses during the door to door verification, and on August 18 it reported that nearly one in three voters of Delhi were likely to be struck off the draft electoral roll.Election Commission figures as on August 31 show that 67.2% of Delhi’s 1,45,10,299 (around 97.5 lakh) registered voters were verified. The remaining 47.5 lakh voters were marked “uncollectable” and categorised as ASDDO voters.Voters whose names are missing from the draft roll will be able to file claims and objections between Aug 31 and Sept 30. During this period, officials will closely examine the claims for inclusion in the electoral roll, while booth-level officers (BLOs) will conduct field visits to verify them. Once the details are found to be in order, the voters’ names will be included in the final SIR electoral roll, scheduled to be published on Nov 4.The SIR exercise was launched on June 30 to update Delhi’s electoral rolls and remove ineligible entries. Originally scheduled to conclude on July 29, it was extended three times. During the exercise, around 13,000 BLOs distributed enumeration forms across all 13 districts, according to Delhi chief electoral officer’s office.Details regarding the assembly wise distribution of the names of deleted voters are awaited.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: How 60-year-old India-Nepal border barrage helped save Bihar from flood
articles.summary: PATNA: On the other side of the India-Nepal border, the Gandak was turning into a force of destruction. Floodwaters surged through Nepal after days of.
articles.body: PATNA: On the other side of the India-Nepal border, the Gandak was turning into a force of destruction. Floodwaters surged through Nepal after days of intense rain and flash flooding, swelling the river system that carries water towards Bihar.Then came the test for a piece of infrastructure built decades ago: The Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage.By Wednesday night, the barrage was handling an extraordinary surge. Its 36 gates were opened as water flowing down from Nepal pushed the Gandak's discharge to around 1.5 lakh cusecs. Yet, by the following morning, the flow had begun to fall and Bihar's embankments had held, easing fears of a devastating inundation across several north Bihar districts.More than 4,000 people were evacuated as a precaution as authorities prepared for the worst. But the feared catastrophe did not unfold on the scale initially feared.The barrage, together with Bihar's network of embankments and round-the-clock monitoring, became a critical line of defence as the flood pulse moved downstream.A river that once brought both life and destructionThe Gandak was never simply an irrigation river. For generations, its floods brought devastation to communities along its course.When India and Nepal signed the Gandak Irrigation and Power Project agreement in Kathmandu on December 4, 1959, the plan was explicitly built around controlling the river and using its waters for irrigation and power. The agreement provided for a barrage, canal head regulators and associated works, with India undertaking construction of the structures in Nepal's territory.The project's logic was simple: Instead of allowing the Gandak to periodically turn into a destructive force, regulate its waters and put them to productive use.When Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated the Gandak-Barrage Project at Bhainsalotan on May 4, 1964, he spoke of precisely that challenge. The Gandak and Kosi, he noted, had benefited the region but had also caused enormous damage, with floods inundating entire villages. The aim of the new barrage was to ensure that the rivers brought benefits without causing the same destruction.The project was designed as much as a symbol of India-Nepal cooperation as a piece of hydraulic engineering.Under the 1959 agreement, India was to construct irrigation canals for Nepal, including the Western Nepal Canal and Eastern Nepal Canal, while also developing a power house in Nepal. The agreement envisaged irrigation benefits across Nepal as well as the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.Six decades later, the river came calling againThe latest flood episode showed why such infrastructure remains crucial.After severe flooding in Nepal, water entered the Gandak system and rapidly raised the threat level in Bihar. All 36 gates of the Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage were opened to regulate the flow. The discharge reached roughly 1.50 lakh cusecs before beginning to recede.The Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage has a designed discharge capacity of up to 8 lakh cusecs. Despite the substantial capacity available, the Gandak Barrage Control Room adopted a calibrated and technically managed release strategy, regulating the discharge in controlled increments in response to changing inflows.This measured approach helped moderate the downstream flood pulse and gave authorities additional time to monitor vulnerable embankments and undertake precautionary evacuations.Eight districts in Bihar were kept on alert, with officials maintaining surveillance of vulnerable embankments. More than 5,000 people were shifted from low-lying areas as a precaution in the initial phase.The crucial point was not that the barrage magically stopped the floodwater. It could not. The water still had to pass downstream.Its importance lay in regulation — giving authorities a massive control point through which the incoming surge could be managed rather than allowing an uncontrolled wall of water to move downstream.An old agreement, a modern flood challengeThe 1959 agreement anticipated precisely the need for cooperation over a river that does not recognise political boundaries.It gave India the authority to execute and maintain project works while preserving Nepal's sovereignty over its territory. It also established arrangements for irrigation, power generation, water withdrawals and sharing shortages.Today, the same cross-border geography makes flood management increasingly complicated.The latest disaster in Nepal sent a surge through the Gandak system, while Bihar had to prepare for the consequences downstream. On August 27, the discharge at Valmikinagar peaked at about 1.50 lakh cusecs before declining. By August 28, the flood threat had receded as the flow fell, with officials saying the situation was under control.The episode is therefore less a story about an old barrage defeating a flood and more a story about infrastructure buying time.Time to open gates.Time to monitor embankments.Time to evacuate villages.Time for the surge to pass.And, ultimately, time for Bihar to avoid the kind of river-driven disaster that once repeatedly ravaged entire settlements.'They only benefit and not cause damage'When Jawaharlal Nehru attended the inauguration of the Gandak-Barrage Project at Bhainsalotan on May 4, 1964, he captured the paradox that had defined the Gandak and Kosi for generations.“These two rivers, the Kosi and the Gandak, have benefited us greatly and at the same time harmed us a great deal too,” Nehru said.“Floods have ravaged the surrounding areas inundating entire villages. Now we want to make arrangements to see that they only benefit and not cause damage.”That, in essence, was the philosophy behind the Gandak project.Nehru explained that the barrage would regulate the river's waters and channel them through canals to agricultural fields. “So, a barrage will be built to dam the waters which will then be supplied through canals to fields all over Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Nepal on the other side,” he said.The project, he added, was not just about controlling water. It was also about transforming the river into an engine of development through irrigation and electricity.“Apart from supplying water for irrigation this river valley project will generate electricity which is a symbol of the new age,” Nehru said.He also described the project as a symbol of cooperation between the two neighbours, saying: “Both Nepal and India stand to gain.”“That is why I am very happy that this auspicious task is being inaugurated by the King of Nepal. It becomes a symbol of Indo-Nepalese cooperation by which both countries stand to gain.”More than six decades later, those words have acquired an unexpected contemporary relevance.The barrage built to ensure that the Gandak's waters would “only benefit and not cause damage” found itself once again at the centre of Bihar's response when floodwaters came rushing downstream from a disaster-ravaged Nepal.The scale of the disaster upstreamThe latest episode also underscored just how severe the situation was on the other side of the border.As flash floods swept through Nepal, rescue teams led by Nepal Army personnel intensified operations to locate hundreds of people missing from flood-hit hydropower projects. At Upper Trishuli-3A, rescuers located the crown head of a tunnel and began widening an opening to send personnel inside with oxygen cylinders.The Independent Power Producers' Association Nepal said 537 workers and staff were unaccounted for across nine projects, while Nepal's disaster management authority, NDRRMA, put the number of missing hydropower workers at 933.By Sunday, the death toll had risen to 810 — 794 in Nepal and 16 reported in Tibet — while 3,048 people were missing across the two countries. NDRRMA listed 2,502 people missing and Tibet another 546.The disaster also had a significant Indian dimension. The Ministry of External Affairs said 149 Indian nationals had been rescued in Nepal. Its latest missing-person tally listed 275 Indian nationals as missing and another 128 people of Indian origin as uncontactable.Against that backdrop, the surge in the Gandak was more than another rise in a river level. It was the downstream consequence of a disaster unfolding across the border.And when the Gandak rose, the decades-old India-Nepal project once again found itself at the centre of Bihar's fight against the water.The river still flowed. The floodwaters still came.But the barrage bought Bihar something invaluable in a flood emergency — time.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news. articles.title: Trojan War fan among 400 conserved at Leeds Discovery Centre
articles.summary: The 350-year-old accessory is among an array of items being cared for at Leeds Discovery Centre.
articles.body:
A 350-year-old fan depicting a pivotal moment from the Greek legend of the Trojan War is part of a collection being cataloged and conserved by experts in Leeds.

Dating back to the 1680s, the folding hand fan is carved from antique ivory, and displays a scene in which the Trojan prince must choose which goddess - Hera, Athena, or Aphrodite - is the most beautiful.

The fan is among 400 items being cared for at Leeds Discovery Centre, with several currently displayed at an exhibition at Lotherton.

Natalie Raw, Leeds Museums and Galleries' curator of costume, said the collection offered a "fascinating insight into how the use of elaborate and beautiful accessories has evolved over the centuries".

"Although today we usually think of fans just being used to help us cool down in the hot weather, in the 18th Century no lady's dress would be complete without one," she said.

"As well as being a beautiful fashion accessory, they were also associated with the idea of flirtation and the imagery painted on them would often signify themes of love and courtship."

The majority of the fans were made in the 18th and 19th centuries, decorated with Greek or Roman mythology, East Asian imagery and other colourful designs.

The archive is predominately made up of fans collected as a hobby by prominent socialites of the day, including Lady Gascoigne of Lotherton and Dorothy Una Ratcliffe who married into the wealthy Brotherton family of West Yorkshire.

Councillor Salma Arif, Leeds City Council's executive member for economy, said the fans were "stunning examples" of fashion and costume that captured the "creativity and imagination of designers through the ages".

"Our whole collection is an incredible archive of millions of years of history and it's wonderful that the people of Leeds are able to visit and be inspired by it," she said.

articles.title: A man who grew up poor and fatherless and barely finished high school went on to open 54 Burger King restaurants across three US states; his foundation has since donated more than $2 million
articles.summary: US News: John Gullo’s story of overcoming a poor, fatherless childhood in a rough Italian neighborhood of Buffalo, New York to becoming a successful businessma.
articles.body: John Gullo’s story of overcoming a poor, fatherless childhood in a rough Italian neighborhood of Buffalo, New York to becoming a successful businessman and philanthropist is a true American success story. According to a Fox Business report, Gullo, now 82, built a career around Burger King, eventually opening 54 restaurants in Utah, Arizona and Wisconsin. His accomplishments included opening what is thought to be the first Burger King attached to a gas station, in Hurricane, Utah.But Gullo’s definition of success has never been about money. He grew up with very little and developed a belief that happiness, service and generosity were more meaningful than wealth. The report states that Gullo got his start as a night manager at Burger King. Over the years he built up his business interests and eventually established a franchise empire in three states. Later, he sold his restaurants, finding he missed working directly with young people and being involved in their development. The next chapter of his life soon focused on his passion for mentoring kids and giving back, adds the Fox Business report.From success to philanthropyIn 2002, Gullo founded the American Dream Foundation, using his business success to benefit charitable causes. For the last 25 years, the foundation has donated more than $2 million to organizations and projects serving children, families, classrooms, firefighters and people with disabilities. Gullo has supported causes such as Prevent Child Abuse, the Children’s Justice Center, Enable Industries, the American Fallen Fire Memorial, Youth in Transition, the Ogden Police Department’s Let’s Play Program and the Treehouse Children’s Museum. The foundation also has helped fund the American Freedom Trail, which gives fifth-graders in Weber County, Utah, a chance to learn about American history and freedom.A memoir built on life lessonsGullo has documented his incredible story in his memoir, Extraordinary Adventures of an Ordinary Man, co-written with author, Bridget Cook-Burch. The book is a mingling of his life story with lessons to inspire young readers. Gullo has stressed the importance of learning from mistakes, taking action and seeing the opportunities life presents. All proceeds from the book are donated to charity, continuing Gullo’s long-standing commitment to giving back.From heart surgery to pickleball pioneerGullo’s influence goes beyond business and philanthropy. In 2008, he had quintuple bypass surgery and then developed heart failure. He learned pickleball. The sport helped him lose 100 pounds and inspired him to grow pickleball in Northern Utah. He helped build hundreds of courts, founded the Professional Pickleball Federation, and created the Tournament of Champions, including prize money he paid out of his own pocket. His work in the sport earned him a spot in the Pickleball Hall of Fame in 2024 and the Father of Professional Pickleball award.Service that connects peopleGullo also has been working with former NBA player Thurl Bailey on charity initiatives over the past 20 years. Their friendship, despite their contrasting backgrounds and differing opinions, is symbolic of Gullo’s larger work to bring people and organizations together through service and community. He credits the Jaycees, a civic and leadership organization for young adults, with helping him overcome his introverted nature and teaching him valuable lessons on leadership, teamwork and community service.An American dream to giveFrom poverty and a high school diploma barely attained, to building 54 restaurants, supporting numerous charities and helping transform pickleball, Gullo's life is proof of a belief that success is measured by more than financial achievement. Ultimately his story is about how one person can create opportunity for others. Having experienced poverty himself, Gullo has spent decades ensuring that children, families and communities have the support and opportunities he didn’t have. The American dream, to Gullo, was never just about making money. It was about building himself up and then using what he built to help others.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: First exam reforms, now 'school thik karo' campaign: How CJP is changing the discourse of politics
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: From colleges to schools. From Gen Z to Gen Alpha. From Jantar Mantar to cities and villages in states. The students’ protest has continued.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: From colleges to schools. From Gen Z to Gen Alpha. From Jantar Mantar to cities and villages in states. The students’ protest has continued; only the stage has shifted. The Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) “School Thik Karo” campaign has put the spotlight on the sorry condition of government schools in many states. Gen Z showed the way from Jantar Mantar when they forced the NDA government to make Dharmendra Pradhan resign over NEET paper leaks. Gen Alpha took the cue and brought the protests to villages and towns across states, demanding better school infrastructure and government accountability.The CJP campaign asking for school audits in villages got a huge response. The pictures and videos of schools uploaded on CJP’s X timeline exposed the sorry state of government schools across states. This was followed by ground inspections by CJP teams, which led to confrontation and a strong pushback by some state governments.Two days after the CJP launched its campaign and announced that schools in Rajasthan would be on its radar, the state education department issued new guidelines regulating the entry of outsiders, including media personnel, into government schools.Under the directives, photography, videography, interviews, audio recording and live streaming involving students or school activities on campus needed prior permission from the school principal or head of the institution. The Rajasthan order went on to threaten action under applicable laws in case of any breach.So, when a CJP team went to inspect a government school on August 21, it was attacked and forcibly pushed back, allegedly by the locals. Videos of the incident showed a large number of people engaging in a heated exchange with the CJP team, pushing and shoving its members as they tried to enter the village. Some clips also showed stone-pelting and smashed windows of cars. Locals said the village did not need outside political groups to intervene in the school’s affairs.This perhaps became the July 20 Jantar Mantar moment (when Delhi Police used force to stop Gen Z protesters from their Sansad march) of the CJP school campaign as the violent confrontation propelled the issue to the national centre stage.School students protest in UPMeanwhile in Uttar Pradesh, Gen Alpha students of a government school staged a protest twice, in a span of four days. over shortage of subject teachers. They briefly blocked traffic also. Students of a government school in Kannauj boycotted classes and held protests against the principal for alleged caste discrimination and ordering the felling of trees inside the school campus. The students of PM Shri Composite School in Gugarapur surrounded the vehicle of the in-charge principal at the school gate as he was leaving and raised slogans against him.Protests also happened in Fatehpur, Hamirpur against lack of facilities in schools. In Hamirpur, 'Gen Alpha' children laid siege to the collectorate to demand the construction of a paved road to their school.In Unnao, hundreds of students of a government-run residential school staged a protest over alleged poor-quality food, inadequate drinking water, shortage of teachers and the behaviour of the principal, briefly disrupting traffic at a city crossing.'Ministers’ dogs got better facilities than students'In Maharashtra, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke conducted a social audit of government-run and municipal schools in Latur district. He led a team at a Zilla Parishad school at Ujani village in Latur's Ausa tehsil.After his audit, Dipke said schools in the state were in a pitiable condition, and even "ministers’ dogs got better facilities" than students. He sought the resignation of Maharashtra school education minister Dada Bhuse. Later, Maharashtra police registered a case against the CJP convenor and others for allegedly entering a government school without permission, disrupting official work and threatening teachers.The state governments cited rules to browbeat the CJP teams away from its schools. But at the same time, they were forced to act to nullify the impact of the CJP campaign. So, while some states announced new measures to improve the condition of schools, others increased the pace of work already underway to ensure that results were seen on the ground quickly.CJP claims creditThe CJP was quick to claim credit for govt actions and basked in glory.“The impact we’ve been able to make with such a small team in such a short span of time is just unreal. Multiple state governments have had to bow down. Authorities had to listen to Gen Z and Gen Alpha kids and give them their due,” it said in a post on X.“But this does not end here. We need to keep going until even the remotest regions of the nation, even the most deprived communities, have access to the highest standard of educational facilities. They may use force, they may file cases, they may do whatever they can to crush this, but we will remain committed to the same demand,” the post read.Political parties take a cue from CJPWhile it can be debated whether or not the CJP campaign forced the governments into action, what can be said with certainty is that the CJP has managed to do what many political parties could not - inspire the youth to come to the streets and seek accountability from power.The two CJP campaigns also point to an interesting shift - which should be a learning lesson, especially for parties in the opposition space. We have seen the opposition parties raise the pitch against government on issues like caste and religion as these have greater potential for voter mobilisation. Rarely do we see campaigns by the opposition parties centred around health or education reforms. But that seems to have changed.Youth outreachThe Congress has taken a cue and is trying to stay focused on students’ connect and raise issues that concern the youth. In Rajasthan, the state Congress unit is also on the streets to highlight gaps in state government school infrastructure.And it’s not just the opposition that is course-correcting; the ruling BJP has also drawn a roadmap to engage with the youth and understand their concerns. In the middle of the Gen Z protest, Prime Minister Narendra Modi debuted on Instagram and tried to communicate directly with the youth who were on the streets. The BJP has in fact formed a dedicated team to spearhead its Gen Z outreach. The team includes BJP chief Nitin Nabin, national general secretaries Smriti Irani and Vinod Tawde, Gujarat minister Harsh Sanghavi, Chhattisgarh minister OP Choudhary, along with several other leaders.Clearly, the CJP has managed to change the political discourse and has put the focus on the youth as potential game-changers in electoral politics. As we gear up for the next rounds of assembly elections in the run-up to the 2029 Lok Sabha challenge, we may see youth outreach taking centre stage like never before.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Hurricane threat in Southern California: 90% chance of disturbance to turn into depression
articles.summary: US News: A tropical disturbance in the eastern Pacific now has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours, while weather models cited by So.
articles.body: A tropical disturbance in the eastern Pacific now has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours, while weather models cited by Southern California meteorologists show it could strengthen into a hurricane later this week before weakening and potentially moving towards the region.The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said the system, designated EP95 — its identifier for the eastern Pacific disturbance being monitored, was well offshore southwestern Mexico late Sunday and moving generally northwest at 10 to 15 mph. Its showers and thunderstorms remained disorganised, but conditions favoured further development.An earlier NHC outlook had put the 48-hour formation chance at 80% and the seven-day probability at 90%, figures cited by National Weather Service (NWS) meteorologist Bryan Lewis. The centre later raised the shorter-term probability to 90%.A tropical depression has maximum sustained winds of 38 mph or less. Under official NHC classifications, a tropical storm has winds of 39 to 73 mph, while hurricane strength begins at 74 mph."Once the depression forms, the National Hurricane Center will then likely write a discussion about it and include probabilities of tropical storm or even hurricane formation, so stay tuned for that," Lewis said.The NHC has not yet issued an official track or intensity forecast for EP95, meaning projections of a hurricane and a possible Southern California approach remain model scenarios rather than an official forecast.Models show possible Southern California approachKaj Goldberg, a meteorologist with KTLA, a Los Angeles television station, said forecasters were closely watching the disturbance. The station said weather prediction models showed a strong possibility of an eye developing off Baja California by Thursday, although the NHC has not forecast an eye forming at this stage. "This is the disturbance that, if it does form and come together, could make its way right into Southern California about one week from today," Goldberg said.He said the system could reach hurricane strength by Friday or Saturday before weakening by Saturday night or early Sunday. Under the scenario discussed by KTLA, it could then move farther north and make landfall in Southern California as a tropical storm.The station said such a track could bring heavy rain and extreme humidity into the following week, with flooding possible.The NWS is more cautious about those potential impacts. Lewis separately told the Los Angeles Times that there was still a high degree of uncertainty over whether the developing system would bring rain to Southern California, although higher surf and stronger rip currents were more likely over the Labor Day weekend.Tropical storm landfalls rare in CaliforniaDirect tropical-storm landfalls from the Pacific are rare in California. An unnamed storm struck near Long Beach in 1939, while Hurricane Nora entered California as a tropical storm in 1997 after first making landfall in Mexico, according to the NWS. "However, several tropical systems have weakened below tropical storm strength before making landfall," Lewis said. "Most recently, Hilary brought significant rainfall and impacts to Southern California in August 2023. Hilary was not a tropical storm by the time it reached California."The NHC's final analysis found that Hilary lost its tropical characteristics over northern Baja California and became post-tropical before moving into Southern California. Despite weakening, it brought significant rainfall and flooding to the region.Karina reaches Category 3 ahead of forecastThe disturbance is developing during an active period in the Pacific. KTLA reported that three storms were contributing to increased swells in Southern California, including Hurricane Karina, which was then a Category 1 storm and was forecast to potentially reach Category 3 by late Monday night or early Tuesday.Karina strengthened much faster. By Sunday evening it had become a Category 3 major hurricane with sustained winds of 125 mph while remaining far offshore and moving westwards. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect, though the NHC said its swells would generate dangerous surf and rip currents along southwestern Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula.The NWS separately warned of a high rip-current risk along Los Angeles County beaches. An earlier Sunday forecast listed surf of up to 6 feet and water temperatures as high as 76 degrees Fahrenheit, while a later update listed temperatures of 71 to 75 degrees.Marine heat wave keeps coastal waters unusually warmKTLA linked the potential storm to a "super" El Niño brewing in the Pacific and noted that the climate pattern is associated with warmer waters in the eastern Pacific.Citing NWS data, it reported sea surface temperatures across Southern California at 5 to 10 degrees above normal for the time of year, with readings of 74 to 76 degrees along Los Angeles County beaches.The relationship between El Niño and the current marine heat wave is more nuanced, however. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has tracked a marine heat wave off central and Southern California since May 2025, before the present El Niño developed. NOAA says more recent warming off Southern California may increasingly reflect El Niño's influence.El Niño has more than 90% chance of becoming very strongEl Niño is characterised by unusually warm waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific and can affect atmospheric circulation and tropical-cyclone activity.The Climate Prediction Center, part of the National Weather Service, says El Niño is strengthening and has a greater than 90% chance of becoming a "very strong event" during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter of 2026-27.The climate pattern can influence conditions in which tropical cyclones develop, but it does not determine the path or strength of an individual storm.For EP95, the next significant development will be the start of NHC advisories if the disturbance becomes sufficiently organised. Those would provide official track and intensity forecasts and indicate whether the modelled Southern California scenario gains or loses support.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
